extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, literature students, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and critical criteria for creating, evaluating, and classifying characters in novels and for choosing the story's point of view; focuses on realism, flat vs round characters, character-plot relations, and narrative vantage point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-as-central_element
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing matters but the character; in some novels (e.g., Moll Flanders) 'a character is everything and is given freest play.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a novel is constructed around a single, dominant person, plot may be perfunctory; evaluate whether the heroine/hero stands 'in an open space' and remains convincing as the principal focus. Example: Defoe's Moll Flanders — slight plot, character occupying the whole book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reality_of_a_character
rubrics_metrics.description: “A character in a book is real when the novelist knows everything about it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The novelist need not tell all facts, but must give the reader the sense that the character is explicable and fully understood by the creator. This quality produces a novelistic reality unavailable in daily life; check for an author's implied omniscience about inner life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel_laws_vs_daily_life_(aesthetic_reply)
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel is a work of art with its own laws; a character is real when it lives in accordance with such laws rather than strictly matching daily life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For examination answers or formal criticism: emphasize that fictional truth rests on internal consistency and convincingness within the book's aesthetic framework (e.g., Emma or Amelia exist only in their worlds). But note limitations — this aesthetic reply may be unsatisfactory for novels where character alone predominates (see Moll).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters_must_acclimatize_to_other_aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must adapt to other requirements of the novel — plot, moral, fellow characters, atmosphere, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how well characters are integrated: are they inter-dependent (as in Jane Austen), or isolated (as in Defoe)? Inter-dependence increases complexity; failure to adapt can make characters 'run away' from the scheme or require authorial checks (killing them off, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallelism_with_daily_life_(not_identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters in most novels need not coincide wholly with daily life but only to parallel it: 'each bit' of a character may coincide with life while the whole parallels it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether character elements match recognizable slices of life while the overall figure remains shaped by the book's needs. Examples: Miss Bates — bits are lifelike but as a whole she is bound to Highbury; Moll can be detached from context more easily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat_character_definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters (formerly 'humours' or 'types') are constructed around a single idea or quality; 'The really flat character can be expressed in one sentence such as "I never will desert Mr. Micawber."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify flatness by test-phraseability: if the person can be summed by one formula and has no existence outside it, they are flat. Use examples (Mrs. Micawber, Caleb Balderstone, many Proust minor figures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages_of_flat_characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters are easily recognized, never need reintroducing, provide their own atmosphere, and are easily remembered — useful conveniences for an author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credit flat characters for efficiency: they function as ready-made counters in the narrative, help with comic effect, and contribute to permanence/refuge quality in literature. They are valuable where quick recognition or repeated effect is desirable (e.g., Dickensian types).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disadvantages_of_flat_characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat people are not in themselves as big achievements as round ones; serious or tragic flat characters are apt to be a bore and cannot sustain prolonged tragic performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat flatness as a limitation where psychological depth or tragic development is required. Critics claiming flatness falsifies life (Norman Douglas's critique) are correct for biography, but in fiction flatness can have a legitimate role; beware boredom when a flat character is treated seriously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round_character_definition_and_test
rubrics_metrics.description: Round characters are complex, capable of surprising in a convincing way; 'The test of a round character is whether it is capable of surprising in a convincing way.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge roundness by convincing unpredictability and internal depth (examples: principal characters in War and Peace, Dostoevsky, Madame Bovary, Becky Sharp). If a surprise feels credible and expands understanding of the character, it indicates roundness; if surprise fails to convince, the character is a flat pretender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional_balance_of_flat_and_round
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel often requires both flat and round characters; using them in combination helps the novelist solve difficulties of scope and keeps the human 'race' harmonized with other aspects of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how an author balances types and fully realized people: Dickens and Wells use mostly flat types energized by authorial force; Austen arranges many smaller but highly organized characters; the mixture can produce vitality even if some figures are schematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character_memory_and_permanence
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters tend to be more easily remembered in a fixed formulaic way and thus help a book endure as a refuge; many readers yearn for permanence in literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a work's 'refuge' quality: does the presence of memorable flat figures (e.g., the Countess in Evan Harrington) contribute to the book's lasting appeal? Contrast with round characters whose remembered identity is tied to events and development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability_and_taste_vs_artistic_improbability
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist may sin only against probability (which is tolerable) but should avoid unnecessary violations of daily life and taste; saying a fictional character literally exists in the real world is 'idiotic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating realism, distinguish between acceptable aesthetic liberties and those that offend taste or plausibility: 'Look out, there’s some one like Moll' is plausible; claiming Moll actually walked in Cambridge is a breach of probability and taste. Use this to critique implausible narrative claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point_of_view_as_fundamental_device
rubrics_metrics.description: The point of view (relation of narrator to story) is a fundamental device: the novelist may describe from outside (impartial/partial onlooker), assume omniscience (describe from within), or place himself as one of the characters (limited/affecting ignorance), among other attitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess which vantage the author adopts and how effectively it ‘bounces’ the reader into accepting the narrative. Point of view affects acclimatization of characters and the reader’s access to secret lives; selecting and executing an appropriate POV is central to the craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiction_as_compensation_for_invisible_private_life
rubrics_metrics.description: Novels can make the secret life visible and offer compensation for the dimness of human intercourse; fiction is truer than history in that it goes beyond evidence to supply inner knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how successfully a novel provides the illusion of perfect knowledge and thereby consoles the reader; measure whether this supplied inner life feels plausible and satisfying even if not strictly factual.
